title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{Triangular structure.}
Order the indices $\alpha\in I_m=\{|\alpha|\le m\}$ by total degree, with
an arbitrary order within each degree. Write $\alpha(1),\ldots,\alpha(q)$
for the ordered indices, where $q=q_m$, write $\zeta_k$ and $\xi_k$ for
the coordinates of $\zeta^{(m)}$ and $\xi^{(m)}$ with index $\alpha(k)$,
and put $\zeta_{<k}=(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_{k-1})$ and
$\xi_{<k}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{k-1})$. By \eqref{eq:triangular-transform},
$\zeta^{(m)}=\sqrt s\,\mathcal T_\theta\xi^{(m)}$ with
$\mathcal T_\theta=e^{-Q_m/(2l^2)}D_{m,l}$. Since $Q_m$ raises total degree
by two, every nonzero entry of $Q_m^r$, $r\ge1$, lies in a row of
strictly higher degree than its column. Hence
$e^{-Q_m/(2l^2)}=\sum_{r\le m/2}(-2l^2)^{-r}Q_m^r/r!$ is unit lower
triangular in this order, and $\mathcal T_\theta$ is lower triangular with
diagonal entries $l^{-|\alpha(k)|}$:
\[
 \zeta_k=\sqrt s\,l^{-|\alpha(k)|}\xi_k
 +\sqrt s\sum_{i<k}(\mathcal T_\theta)_{ki}\,\xi_i,
 \qquad k=1,\ldots,q.
\]
The leading $(k-1)\times(k-1)$ block of $\mathcal T_\theta$ is invertible,
so $\zeta_{<k}$ and $\xi_{<k}$ are invertible linear functions of each
other, and $\xi_k$ is independent of $\xi_{<k}$. Therefore, under
$P_\theta$, the conditional law of $\zeta_k$ given $\zeta_{<k}$ is
$N(\mu_{\theta,k}(\zeta_{<k}),\omega_{\theta,k})$, where $\mu_{\theta,k}$ is a
linear function of $\zeta_{<k}$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:conditional-variance}
 \omega_{\theta,k}=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\zeta_k\mid\zeta_{<k})
 =s\,l^{-2|\alpha(k)|}.
\end{equation}
The conditional variance does not depend on $\zeta_{<k}$.

\textbf{Univariate affinity.}
For normal densities with means $\mu,\mu'$ and variances $\omega,\omega'$, the
exponent of the product of the two square roots satisfies
\[
 -\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{4\omega}-\frac{(x-\mu')^2}{4\omega'}
 =-\frac{(x-\bar\mu)^2}{2w}-\frac{(\mu-\mu')^2}{4(\omega+\omega')},
 \qquad w=\frac{2\omega\omega'}{\omega+\omega'},
\]
for a suitable $\bar\mu$. Integrating with respect to $x$ gives
\begin{align*}
 \operatorname{Aff}\{N(\mu,\omega),N(\mu',\omega')\}
 &=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi w}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,(\omega\omega')^{1/4}}
 \exp\Bigl\{-\frac{(\mu-\mu')^2}{4(\omega+\omega')}\Bigr\} =\left(\frac{2\sqrt{\omega\omega'}}{\omega+\omega'}\right)^{1/2}
   \exp\left\{-\frac{(\mu-\mu')^2}{4(\omega+\omega')}\right\}.
\end{align*}
Since $(\omega+\omega')/(2\sqrt{\omega\omega'})
=\frac12(\sqrt{\omega/\omega'}+\sqrt{\omega'/\omega})
=\cosh\{\frac12\log(\omega/\omega')\}$, it follows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:univariate-affinity}
 \operatorname{Aff}\{N(\mu,\omega),N(\mu',\omega')\}
 \le\cosh\Bigl\{\frac12\log\frac\omega{\omega'}\Bigr\}^{-1/2}
 \qquad\text{for all }\mu,\mu'.
\end{equation}

\textbf{Successive integration.}
Let $\pi_\theta$ denote the density of $\zeta^{(m)}$ under $P_\theta$, and
$\pi_\theta(\zeta_k\mid\zeta_{<k})$ its conditional densities, so that
$\pi_\theta(\zeta)=\prod_{k=1}^q\pi_\theta(\zeta_k\mid\zeta_{<k})$. For
$0\le k\le q$ put
\[
 \mathcal A_k=\int_{\mathbb R^k}\prod_{i=1}^k
 \sqrt{\pi_\theta(\zeta_i\mid\zeta_{<i})\,
 \pi_{\theta_0}(\zeta_i\mid\zeta_{<i})}\;d\zeta_1\cdots d\zeta_k,
\]
so that $\mathcal A_0=1$ and
$\mathcal A_q=\operatorname{Aff}(\Sigma_{m,\theta},\Sigma_{m,\theta_0})$. The integrand is
nonnegative, so by Tonelli's theorem we may integrate over $\zeta_k$
first, with $\zeta_{<k}$ fixed. By \eqref{eq:univariate-affinity},
\[
 \int_\mathbb R\sqrt{\pi_\theta(\zeta_k\mid\zeta_{<k})\,
 \pi_{\theta_0}(\zeta_k\mid\zeta_{<k})}\;d\zeta_k
 \le\rho_k:=\cosh\Bigl\{\frac12\log\frac{\omega_{\theta,k}}{\omega_{\theta_0,k}}\Bigr\}^{-1/2}.
\]
This bound is the same for every value of $\zeta_{<k}$, because the
conditional variances \eqref{eq:conditional-variance} do not depend on
$\zeta_{<k}$. The conditional means, which do depend on $\zeta_{<k}$ and
on the parameter, enter only through the exponential factor of the
univariate affinity, which is at most one. Hence
$\mathcal A_k\le\rho_k\mathcal A_{k-1}$, and by induction
$\operatorname{Aff}(\Sigma_{m,\theta},\Sigma_{m,\theta_0})\le\prod_{k=1}^q\rho_k$.
Finally, with $u=\log(s/s_0)$ and $v=\log(l/l_0)$,
\eqref{eq:conditional-variance} gives
$\log(\omega_{\theta,k}/\omega_{\theta_0,k})=u-2|\alpha(k)|v$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coefficient-affinity-product}
 \operatorname{Aff}(\Sigma_{m,\theta},\Sigma_{m,\theta_0})
 \le\prod_{k=1}^q\cosh\bigl(u/2-|\alpha(k)|v\bigr)^{-1/2}
 =\exp\left\{-\frac12\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}
             \log\cosh(u/2-|\alpha|v)\right\}.
\end{equation}

\textbf{A fixed fraction of separated degrees.}
To bound the sum, select a multiindex $\alpha$ uniformly from $I_m$, let
$J=|\alpha|$, and put $Z=J/m$ for $m\ge1$. The number of indices of degree
$j$ is $\binom{j+p-1}{p-1}$. Binomial summation gives
\[
 \mathbb E Z=\frac{p}{p+1},\qquad
 \mathbb E Z^2=\frac{p}{p+2}
       +\frac{p}{(p+1)(p+2)m}.
\]
The matrix
$\mathbb M=\begin{pmatrix}1&-\mathbb E Z\\-\mathbb E Z&\mathbb E Z^2\end{pmatrix}$ has
$\det\mathbb M=\operatorname{Var} Z\ge\frac p{p+2}-\frac{p^2}{(p+1)^2}
=\frac p{(p+2)(p+1)^2}$ and $\operatorname{tr}\mathbb M\le2$, so
\[
 \lambda_{\min}(\mathbb M)\ge\frac{\det\mathbb M}{\operatorname{tr}\mathbb M}
 \ge c_p:=\frac p{2(p+2)(p+1)^2}.
\]
Put $a=u/2$, $b=mv$, and $L_0=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, so that
$a-bZ=u/2-|\alpha|v$. Then
\[
 \mathbb E(a-bZ)^2=a^2-2ab\,\mathbb E Z+b^2\mathbb E Z^2
 =(a,b)\,\mathbb M\,(a,b)^\top\ge c_pL_0^2,
\]
and, since $0\le Z\le1$, $|a-bZ|\le|a|+|b|\le\sqrt2L_0$. If $L_0=0$, then
$u=v=0$ and \eqref{eq:degree-separation} below is trivial. Otherwise,
\Cref{lem:fraction} with $X=a-bZ$, $\sigma^2=c_pL_0^2$, $M=\sqrt2L_0$, and
$\lambda=1/\sqrt2$ shows that the set
\[
 \mathcal G=\bigl\{\alpha\in I_m:|u/2-|\alpha|v|\ge c_0L_0\bigr\},
 \qquad c_0=(c_p/2)^{1/2},
\]
contains at least $(c_p/4)q_m\ge(c_p/4)m^p/p!$ indices.

\textbf{Lower bound for the sum.} For all real $z$,
\begin{equation*}
 \log\cosh(1)\min(z^2,|z|)\le\log\cosh z\le\min(z^2/2,|z|).
\end{equation*}
The upper bound is elementary. For the lower bound, the function
$g(z)=2\log\cosh z-z\tanh z$ satisfies $g(0)=0$ and
$g'(z)=\operatorname{sech}^2z\,(\tfrac12\sinh2z-z)\ge0$ for $z\ge0$, so
$(\log\cosh z)/z^2$ is nonincreasing on $(0,\infty)$; this gives the
bound for $|z|\le1$. For $|z|\ge1$, it follows from convexity of
$\log\cosh$ and $\log\cosh0=0$. For $\alpha\in\mathcal G$, since
$\log\cosh$ is increasing in $|z|$ and $c_0\le1$,
\[
 \log\cosh(u/2-|\alpha|v)\ge\log\cosh(c_0L_0)
 \ge\log\cosh(1)\,c_0^2\min(L_0^2,L_0).
\]
Since $L_0^2\ge(u^2+m^2v^2)/4$, we have
$\min(L_0^2,L_0)\ge\frac14\min\{u^2+m^2v^2,(u^2+m^2v^2)^{1/2}\}$.
Discarding the nonnegative terms with $\alpha\notin\mathcal G$ and using
$|\mathcal G|\ge(c_p/4)m^p/p!$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:degree-separation}
 \sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\log\cosh(u/2-|\alpha|v)
 \ge cm^p\min\bigl\{u^2+m^2v^2,(u^2+m^2v^2)^{1/2}\bigr\}.
\end{equation}

By \Cref{lem:affinity-monotone}, the affinity of the observation laws
is at most the affinity of the laws of the parameter-independent linear
statistic $H_nY_n$. By \Cref{lem:recovery}, the latter log affinity differs from that of the exact
coefficient vector by $o(1)$, uniformly over the parameters. Combining
this fact with \eqref{eq:coefficient-affinity-product},
\eqref{eq:degree-separation}, and $m_n\asymp b_n$ proves
\eqref{eq:affinity-separation}. The coefficient law has no nugget
parameter, and its recovery bound is uniform in $t$; this proves the
claimed uniformity in the nugget as well.

We now prove \eqref{eq:affinity-joint}. On the rectangle, the mean value
theorem gives $|\log(s/s_0)|\ge|s-s_0|/s_+$ and
$|\log(l/l_0)|\ge|l-l_0|/l_+$. Hence, with
$c_1=\min\{1,s_+^{-2},l_+^{-2}\}$,
\[
 \Lambda_n(\theta)^2
 \ge c_1\{(s-s_0)^2+b_n^2(l-l_0)^2\}
 =c_1b_n^{-p}\left\lVerth_\mathrm{sp}\right\rVert^2 .
\]
Since $x\mapsto\min(x^2,x)$ is increasing on $[0,\infty)$,
\[
 b_n^p\min\{\Lambda_n(\theta)^2,\Lambda_n(\theta)\}
 \ge\min\bigl\{c_1\left\lVerth_\mathrm{sp}\right\rVert^2,c_1^{1/2}b_n^{p/2}\left\lVerth_\mathrm{sp}\right\rVert\bigr\}
 \ge c_1\min\bigl(\left\lVerth_\mathrm{sp}\right\rVert^2,b_n^{p/2}\left\lVerth_\mathrm{sp}\right\rVert\bigr),
\]
and \eqref{eq:affinity-separation} gives
$\operatorname{Aff}(P_{\theta,n},P_{\theta_0,n})
\le\exp\{e_n-cc_1\min(\left\lVerth_\mathrm{sp}\right\rVert^2,b_n^{p/2}\left\lVerth_\mathrm{sp}\right\rVert)\}$.

For the nugget, use the noise block $W_n=V_n^\top Y_n$ of
\eqref{eq:block-notation}. Since $P_nV_n=0$,
$\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(W_n)=tI_{d_n}+E_\theta$ with
$E_\theta=V_n^\top S_n(\theta)V_n
=V_n^\top\{S_n(\theta)-P_nS_n(\theta)P_n\}V_n$. By
\eqref{eq:projection-approx}, $0\preceq E_\theta\preceq n^{-20}I_{d_n}$
for all $\theta\in\Theta$. Therefore the eigenvalues
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{d_n}$ of
$\operatorname{Cov}_{\theta_0}(W_n)^{-1/2}\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(W_n)\operatorname{Cov}_{\theta_0}(W_n)^{-1/2}$
satisfy $|\log\lambda_k-\log(t/t_0)|\le n^{-20}/t_-$. By
\eqref{eq:gaussian-affinity},
\[
 -\log\operatorname{Aff}\{\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(W_n),\operatorname{Cov}_{\theta_0}(W_n)\}
 =\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{d_n}\log\cosh\Bigl(\frac12\log\lambda_k\Bigr).
\]
The function $y\mapsto\log\cosh(y/2)$ is $\tfrac12$-Lipschitz, and since
its second derivative is $\frac14\operatorname{sech}^2(y/2)$, it is at
least $c_2y^2$ for $|y|\le\log(t_+/t_-)$, where
$c_2=\frac18\operatorname{sech}^2\{\frac12\log(t_+/t_-)\}$. Using
$|\log(t/t_0)|\ge|t-t_0|/t_+$, $d_n\le n$, and $d_n\ge n/2$ for large $n$,
\[
 -\log\operatorname{Aff}\{\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(W_n),\operatorname{Cov}_{\theta_0}(W_n)\}
 \ge\frac{c_2}{4t_+^2}\,n(t-t_0)^2-\frac{n^{-19}}{t_-}
 =\frac{c_2}{4t_+^2}\,h_t^2-\frac{n^{-19}}{t_-}.
\]
The statistic $W_n=V_n^\top Y_n$ is linear and parameter independent, so
\Cref{lem:affinity-monotone} shows that the affinity of the observation
laws is at most this affinity. Since
$\min(e^{-x},e^{-y})\le e^{-(x+y)/2}$, the spatial and nugget bounds
together prove \eqref{eq:affinity-joint}, with $c$ replaced by
$\frac12\min\{cc_1,c_2/(4t_+^2)\}$ and $e_n$ by $\max(e_n,n^{-19}/t_-)$.
The design enters only through \Cref{lem:projection,lem:recovery}. Their
constants depend on $\mathcal X$, $Q$, $C_h$, and $\kappa$, and their proofs use
\eqref{eq:coverage} only at the current $n$. No constant depends on
$\theta_0$: the bounds of \Cref{lem:recovery} hold uniformly over pairs
$\theta,\theta'\in\Theta$, and the remaining constants depend only on
$p$ and the endpoints of $\Theta$.

body_md:
The matrix $C_n(\theta)$ is a smooth positive definite function of
$\theta$ on a neighborhood of $\Theta$, so $l_n$ is continuously
differentiable there and $\xi_n$ has continuous paths. Write
$\theta_h=\theta_0+D_n^{-1}h$ and
$\nabla_hl_n(h)=D_n^{-1}(\nabla l_n)(\theta_h)$. Since $Z_n(h)$ is
the density of $P_{\theta_h,n}$ with respect to $P_{\theta_0,n}$,
\[
 \mathbb E_{\theta_0,n}\xi_n(h)^m=\mathbb E_{\theta_0,n}Z_n(h)^{1/2}
 =\int\sqrt{dP_{\theta_h,n}\,dP_{\theta_0,n}},
\]
which is \eqref{eq:lr-moment}.

For \eqref{eq:lr-lipschitz}, let $u,v\in U_n$ and $w_r=v+r(u-v)$ for
$r\in[0,1]$; these points lie in the box $U_n$. Since
$\frac{d}{dr}\xi_n(w_r)=(2m)^{-1}\xi_n(w_r)\nabla_hl_n(w_r)^\top(u-v)$,
Minkowski's integral inequality gives
\[
 \left\lVert\xi_n(u)-\xi_n(v)\right\rVert_{L^m}
 \le\frac{\left\lVertu-v\right\rVert}{2m}\sup_{w\in U_n}
 \bigl(\mathbb E_{\theta_0,n}[Z_n(w)^{1/2}\left\lVert\nabla_hl_n(w)\right\rVert^m]\bigr)^{1/m}.
\]
Fix $w$ and abbreviate $\theta=\theta_w$. Changing measure and applying
the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality under $P_{\theta,n}$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{\theta_0,n}\bigl[Z_n(w)^{1/2}\left\lVert\nabla_hl_n(w)\right\rVert^m\bigr]
 &=\mathbb E_{\theta,n}\bigl[Z_n(w)^{-1/2}\left\lVert\nabla_hl_n(w)\right\rVert^m\bigr]\\
 &\le\bigl(\mathbb E_{\theta,n}Z_n(w)^{-1}\bigr)^{1/2}
 \bigl(\mathbb E_{\theta,n}\left\lVert\nabla_hl_n(w)\right\rVert^{2m}\bigr)^{1/2},
\end{aligned}
\]
and $\mathbb E_{\theta,n}Z_n(w)^{-1}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0,n}1=1$. Under $P_{\theta,n}$,
$X=C_n(\theta)^{-1/2}Y_n\sim N_n(0,I_n)$, and the coordinates of
$\nabla_hl_n(w)$ are $\frac12\{X^\top B_a(\theta)X-\operatorname{tr} B_a(\theta)\}$
for $a\in\{s,l,t\}$, where
$B_a(\theta)=D_{n,aa}^{-1}C_n(\theta)^{-1/2}C_{n,a}(\theta)C_n(\theta)^{-1/2}$.
Dividing \eqref{eq:raw-frobenius} by $D_{n,aa}$ gives
$\left\lVertB_a(\theta)\right\rVert_\mathrm F\le C$ for $a\in\{s,l\}$, uniformly over
$\theta\in\Theta$ and $n$, and
$\left\lVertB_t(\theta)\right\rVert_\mathrm F=n^{-1/2}\left\lVertC_n(\theta)^{-1}\right\rVert_\mathrm F\le t_-^{-1}$.
\Cref{lem:qf-moments} therefore gives
$\mathbb E_{\theta,n}\left\lVert\nabla_hl_n(w)\right\rVert^{2m}\le C$, uniformly in $w$ and
$n$, which proves \eqref{eq:lr-lipschitz}.

\Cref{lem:lr-process} on the box $U_n=D_n(\Theta-\theta_0)$. Write
$u=(u_1,u_2)$, where $u_1\in\mathbb R^2$ holds the spatial coordinates and
$u_2\in\mathbb R$ the nugget coordinate. Let $n$ be large enough that $b_n\ge1$. By
\eqref{eq:lr-moment} and \eqref{eq:affinity-joint}, the envelope
\eqref{eq:envelope-moment} holds with $A=\exp(\sup_ne_n)$, with $a$ equal
to the constant $c$ of \eqref{eq:affinity-joint}, and with
$\gamma_1=b_n^{p/2}$ and $\gamma_2=\infty$. By \eqref{eq:lr-lipschitz},
\eqref{eq:envelope-lipschitz} holds with $B=C_L$. These constants do not
depend on $n$.

Since $\widehat\theta_n$ maximizes $l_n$ over $\Theta$,
$\xi_n(\widehat h_n)\ge\xi_n(0)=1$. Hence Markov's inequality and
\Cref{cor:envelope} with $(H_1,H_2)=(H,0)$ give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb P\{\left\lVert\widehat h_{n,\mathrm{sp}}\right\rVert\ge H\}
 &\le\mathbb P\Bigl\{\sup_{u\in U_n,\,|u_1|\ge H}\xi_n(u)\ge1\Bigr\}
 \le\mathbb E\sup_{u\in U_n,\,|u_1|\ge H}\xi_n(u)^m\\
 &\le C\exp\{-a''\min(H^2,b_n^{p/2}H)\},
\end{aligned}

$\mathbb P\{|\widehat h_{n,t}|\ge H\}\le C\exp(-a''H^2)$.

\Cref{cor:envelope}, which do not depend on the box $U_n$. The design

title: Proof
body_md:
The spatial upper bounds follow from
\eqref{eq:fisher} and the first derivative Frobenius bounds in
\Cref{lem:projection}. The nugget upper bound follows from
$C_n^{-1}\preceq t_-^{-1}I_n$.

\textbf{Spatial lower bound.}
Write $D_{n,\mathrm{sp}}=\operatorname{diag}(b_n^{p/2},b_n^{p/2+1})$.
For $\left\lVerth\right\rVert\le1$ in $\mathbb R^2$, set
$\theta_h=((s_0,l_0)+D_{n,\mathrm{sp}}^{-1}h,t_0)$ and
\[
 E_n(h)=C_{n,0}^{-1/2}
       \{C_n(\theta_h)-C_{n,0}\}C_{n,0}^{-1/2}.
\]
For $a\in\{s,l\}$, let
$B_{n,a}=D_{n,aa}^{-1}C_{n,0}^{-1/2}C_{n,a}(\theta_0)C_{n,0}^{-1/2}$ be the
normalized whitened first derivatives at $\theta_0$.

\textbf{Covariance comparability.}
Fix $h$ with $\left\lVerth\right\rVert\le1$, put $C(u)=C_n(\theta_{uh})$ for $u\in[0,1]$,
and fix $x\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. The function $f(u)=x^\top C(u)x$ is
positive, and
\[
 f'(u)=\sum_{a\in\{s,l\}}h_aD_{n,aa}^{-1}\,x^\top C_{n,a}(\theta_{uh})x
 =\sum_{a\in\{s,l\}}h_a\,y^\top\widetilde B_a(u)y,
\]
where $y=C(u)^{1/2}x$ and
$\widetilde B_a(u)=D_{n,aa}^{-1}C(u)^{-1/2}C_{n,a}(\theta_{uh})C(u)^{-1/2}$.
Here the whitening is at the same parameter as the derivative, so
dividing \eqref{eq:raw-operator} by $D_{n,aa}$ gives
$\left\lVert\widetilde B_a(u)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\epsilon_n$, uniformly in $u$ and $h$.
Since $|h_s|+|h_l|\le\sqrt2$ and $\left\lVerty\right\rVert^2=f(u)$,
\[
 |f'(u)|\le\sqrt2\,C\epsilon_n f(u),
 \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad
 \Bigl|\frac{d}{du}\log f(u)\Bigr|\le\sqrt2\,C\epsilon_n.
\]
Integrating over $[0,u]$ gives
$e^{-\sqrt2C\epsilon_n}f(0)\le f(u)\le e^{\sqrt2C\epsilon_n}f(0)$. Since $x$ was
arbitrary, after renaming the constant,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:info-comparability}
 e^{-C\epsilon_n}C_{n,0}\preceq C_n(\theta_{uh})\preceq e^{C\epsilon_n}C_{n,0},
 \qquad u\in[0,1],\ \left\lVerth\right\rVert\le1.
\end{equation}

\textbf{Change of whitening.}
Let $K(u)=C_{n,0}^{-1/2}C(u)^{1/2}$. Then
$\left\lVertK(u)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^2=\left\lVertC_{n,0}^{-1/2}C(u)C_{n,0}^{-1/2}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$, which
is at most $e^{C\epsilon_n}$ by \eqref{eq:info-comparability}. For any
$n\times n$ matrix $A$,
\[
 C_{n,0}^{-1/2}AC_{n,0}^{-1/2}=K(u)\{C(u)^{-1/2}AC(u)^{-1/2}\}K(u)^\top,
\]
so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rewhitening}
 \left\lVertC_{n,0}^{-1/2}AC_{n,0}^{-1/2}\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}
 \le e^{C\epsilon_n}\left\lVertC(u)^{-1/2}AC(u)^{-1/2}\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}.
\end{equation}

\textbf{Taylor expansion.}
Taylor's formula with integral remainder, applied to $u\mapsto C(u)$,
gives $E_n(h)=h_sB_{n,s}+h_lB_{n,l}+R_n(h)$ with
\[
 R_n(h)=\int_0^1(1-u)\,C_{n,0}^{-1/2}C''(u)\,C_{n,0}^{-1/2}\,du,
 \qquad
 C''(u)=\sum_{a,b\in\{s,l\}}h_ah_bD_{n,aa}^{-1}D_{n,bb}^{-1}
 C_{n,ab}(\theta_{uh}).
\]
By \Cref{lem:projection}, the normalized second derivatives whitened at
$\theta_{uh}$ have Frobenius norm $O(\epsilon_n)$, so
$\left\lVertC(u)^{-1/2}C''(u)C(u)^{-1/2}\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}=O(\epsilon_n)$. By
\eqref{eq:rewhitening}, the same holds after whitening at $C_{n,0}$, and
therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-increment}
 E_n(h)=h_sB_{n,s}+h_lB_{n,l}+R_n(h),\quad
 \sup_{\left\lVerth\right\rVert\le1}\left\lVertR_n(h)\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}=O(\epsilon_n).
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\left\lVertB_{n,a}\right\rVert_\mathrm F\le C$ by \Cref{lem:projection}, so
$\left\lVertE_n(h)\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}=O(1)$, and \eqref{eq:info-comparability} with
$u=1$ places every eigenvalue of $E_n(h)$ in
$[e^{-C\epsilon_n}-1,e^{C\epsilon_n}-1]$, so
$\left\lVertE_n(h)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=O(\epsilon_n)$, uniformly on $\left\lVerth\right\rVert\le1$.

For any symmetric $E$ with small operator norm,
\[
 \frac12\log\det(I+E/2)-\frac14\log\det(I+E)
 =\frac1{16}\operatorname{tr}(E^2)
  +O(\left\lVertE\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\left\lVertE\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2).
\]
By \eqref{eq:gaussian-affinity} and \eqref{eq:relative-increment},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-affinity-expansion}
 -\log\operatorname{Aff}(P_{\theta_h,n},P_{\theta_0,n})
 =\frac18h^\top J_{n,\mathrm{sp}}h+o(1)
\end{equation}
uniformly on $\left\lVerth\right\rVert\le1$.

For $\left\lVerth\right\rVert=1$, the point $\theta_h$ has rescaled coordinates
$(h,0)$, with spatial part $h$ and nugget part $0$. Hence
\eqref{eq:affinity-joint} gives, once $b_n\ge1$,
\[
 -\log\operatorname{Aff}(P_{\theta_h,n},P_{\theta_0,n})
 \ge c\min(1,b_n^{p/2})-e_n=c-e_n.
\]
Comparing with \eqref{eq:local-affinity-expansion}, we obtain
$\frac18h^\top J_{n,\mathrm{sp}}h\ge c-o(1)$ uniformly on the unit circle, so
$J_{n,\mathrm{sp}}\succeq4cI_2$ for all sufficiently large $n$. This argument uses a finite local
shift and does not differentiate the coefficient recovery error.

\textbf{Nugget block and cross information.}
By \Cref{lem:projection}, the positive signal covariance $S_n(\theta_0)$
has at most $r_n=O(b_n^p)$ eigenvalues exceeding $n^{-20}$.
Therefore
\[
 \frac{\mathcal I_{tt,n}(\theta_0)}n
 =\frac1{2n}\operatorname{tr}(C_{n,0}^{-2})
 \longrightarrow\frac1{2t_0^2}.
\]
For $a=s,l$, approximate the normalized whitened derivative $B_{n,a}$
by a matrix $B_{n,a}^{(r)}$ of rank at most $r_n$, using the same
projection. Its Frobenius norm is bounded and the discarded part is
negligible in all traces below. The normalized nugget derivative is
$B_{n,t}=C_{n,0}^{-1}/\sqrt n$, so
\[
 |J_{n,at}|
 \le\frac12\left\lVertB_{n,t}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
      \left\lVertB_{n,a}^{(r)}\right\rVert_*
      +o(1)
 \le C\sqrt{\frac{r_n}{n}}+o(1)=o(1),
\]
where $\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_*$ is the sum of singular values and
$\left\lVertB^{(r)}\right\rVert_*\le\sqrt{r_n}\left\lVertB^{(r)}\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}$.
The spatial lower bound and the nugget limit establish
\eqref{eq:information-bounds} and \eqref{eq:information-block}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $X_n=C_{n,0}^{-1/2}Y_n\sim N_n(0,I_n)$.
Define, for $a,b\in\{s,l,t\}$,
\[
 B_a=\frac{C_{n,0}^{-1/2}C_{n,a}(\theta_0)C_{n,0}^{-1/2}}{D_{n,aa}},
 \quad
 B_{ab}=
 \frac{C_{n,0}^{-1/2}C_{n,ab}(\theta_0)C_{n,0}^{-1/2}}
 {D_{n,aa}D_{n,bb}}.
\]
The Gaussian score is
\[
 \Delta_{n,a}=\frac12\{X_n^\top B_aX_n-\operatorname{tr} B_a\}.
\]
It has mean zero and covariance
$J_{n,ab}=\frac12\operatorname{tr}(B_aB_b)$.

Directly differentiating the likelihood gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:centered-hessian}
 [\nabla_h^2L_n(0)+J_n]_{ab}
 =\frac12\{X_n^\top M_{ab}X_n-\operatorname{tr} M_{ab}\},
 \quad M_{ab}=B_{ab}-B_aB_b-B_bB_a.
\end{equation}
\Cref{lem:projection} gives
$\left\lVertB_a\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\epsilon_n$,
$\left\lVertB_a\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}\le C$, and
$\left\lVertB_{ab}\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}\le C\epsilon_n$; the nugget's operator
bound is smaller, and second derivatives involving it are zero.
Thus $\left\lVertM_{ab}\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}\le C\epsilon_n$.
For a symmetric matrix $M$,
$\operatorname{Var}(X_n^\top MX_n)=2\left\lVertM\right\rVert_{\mathrm F}^2$.
Equation \eqref{eq:centered-hessian} proves \eqref{eq:hessian-local}.

\textbf{Uniform third derivatives in the signal block.}
Use the fixed subspace and covariance $A_\theta$ from
\eqref{eq:block-notation}. Compression preserves the relative derivative
bounds in \Cref{lem:projection}. In particular, every nonzero covariance
derivative of total order $k\le3$ in $h$ has relative operator norm
at most $C\epsilon_n^k$. A first nugget derivative is bounded by
$Cn^{-1/2}\le C\epsilon_n$, and higher covariance derivatives involving
the nugget vanish.

For $\left\lVerth\right\rVert\le H_n$, integration of the first
relative derivative bound along the segment from $0$ to $h$, exactly as
in the proof of \eqref{eq:info-comparability}, gives
\begin{equation*}
 e^{-C\epsilon_nH_n}A_{\theta_0}
 \preceq A_{\theta_0+D_n^{-1}h}
 \preceq e^{C\epsilon_nH_n}A_{\theta_0}.
\end{equation*}
Since $\epsilon_nH_n\to0$ and
$Z_n^\top A_{\theta_0}^{-1}Z_n\sim\chi_{r_n}^2$,
\begin{equation*}
 \sup_{\left\lVerth\right\rVert\le H_n}
 Z_n^\top A_{\theta_0+D_n^{-1}h}^{-1}Z_n=O_{\mathbb P}(r_n).
\end{equation*}
This bounds the entire neighborhood using the same random quadratic form.

Every third derivative of
$-\frac12\log\det A_\theta-\frac12Z_n^\top A_\theta^{-1}Z_n$
is a finite sum of traces or quadratic forms formed from products of
whitened covariance derivatives of total order three. Each product has
operator norm at most $C\epsilon_n^3$. The traces are bounded by
$Cr_n\epsilon_n^3$, and the quadratic forms by
$C\epsilon_n^3Z_n^\top A_\theta^{-1}Z_n$. Therefore,
\[
 \sup_{\left\lVerth\right\rVert\le H_n}\max_{a,b,c}
 |\partial_{h_ah_bh_c}^3\widetilde L_{n,\mathrm{signal}}(h)|
 \le C\epsilon_n^3
 \left(r_n+\sup_{\left\lVerth\right\rVert\le H_n}Z_n^\top A_\theta^{-1}Z_n\right)
 =O_{\mathbb P}(\epsilon_n),
\]
because $r_n=O(b_n^p)=O(\epsilon_n^{-2})$.

In the complementary block, the log likelihood is
$-\frac12d_n\log t-\left\lVertW_n\right\rVert^2/(2t)$. Only derivatives in $h_t$
are nonzero. Its third derivative is bounded by
$Cn^{-3/2}(d_n+\left\lVertW_n\right\rVert^2)=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})$ uniformly on the
local ball. The exact likelihood derivative differs by
$O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-16})$ from this reduced likelihood derivative, by
\eqref{eq:likelihood-approx}; normalization only decreases that error.
This proves \eqref{eq:third-local}.

The interior assumption and
$H_n\left\lVertD_n^{-1}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=\epsilon_nH_n\to0$ ensure admissibility of the
whole ball. Since $\nabla_hL_n(0)=\Delta_n$, Taylor's formula gives, for
$\left\lVerth\right\rVert\le H_n$,
\[
 L_n(h)-L_n(0)-h^\top\Delta_n+\frac12h^\top J_nh
 =\frac12h^\top\{\nabla_h^2L_n(0)+J_n\}h
 +\frac16\sum_{a,b,c}\partial^3_{h_ah_bh_c}L_n(\bar h)\,h_ah_bh_c
\]
for some $\bar h$ on the segment from $0$ to $h$. By
\eqref{eq:hessian-local}, \eqref{eq:third-local}, and
$\sum_a|h_a|\le\sqrt3\left\lVerth\right\rVert$, the right side is
$O_{\mathbb P}(\epsilon_nH_n^2+\epsilon_nH_n^3)=O_{\mathbb P}(\epsilon_nH_n^3)$ uniformly
on the ball, because $H_n\ge1$. This proves \eqref{eq:quadratic-remainder},
and \eqref{eq:uniform-quadratic} follows.

\textbf{Sharpness (\Cref{rem:radius}).}
Along the variance direction $h=ue_s$, the covariance is
$C(\sigma)=\sigma R_n(l_0)+t_0I_n$ with $\sigma=s_0+b_n^{-p/2}u$, so
$\partial_\sigma C=R_n(l_0)$ and $\partial_\sigma^2C=0$. Differentiating
$l=-\frac12\log\det C-\frac12Y_n^\top C^{-1}Y_n$ gives $\partial_\sigma^3l = -\operatorname{tr}\{(C^{-1}R_n)^3\}+3Y_n^\top C^{-1}(R_nC^{-1})^3Y_n$ and $\partial_\sigma^4l = 3\operatorname{tr}\{(C^{-1}R_n)^4\}-12Y_n^\top C^{-1}(R_nC^{-1})^4Y_n$,
               
                                                                                
                        
                                                                               
             
with $R_n=R_n(l_0)$. At $u=0$, in terms of $X_n=C_{n,0}^{-1/2}Y_n$ and
the normalized derivative $B_s$,
$\partial_{h_s}^3L_n(0)=-\operatorname{tr}(B_s^3)+3X_n^\top B_s^3X_n$. Its mean is
$2\operatorname{tr}(B_s^3)$, and its standard deviation is
$3\sqrt2\left\lVertB_s^3\right\rVert_\mathrm F\le C\left\lVertB_s\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^2\left\lVertB_s\right\rVert_\mathrm F
\le C\epsilon_n^2$ by \Cref{lem:projection}. The matrix $B_s$ is positive
semidefinite. By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality over its eigenvalues,
$(\operatorname{tr} B_s^2)^2\le\operatorname{tr}(B_s)\operatorname{tr}(B_s^3)$. Here $\operatorname{tr} B_s^2=2J_{n,ss}\ge2c$ by
\Cref{lem:information}. Moreover, $B_s=b_n^{-p/2}R_n(s_0R_n+t_0I_n)^{-1}$
has eigenvalues $b_n^{-p/2}\mu/(s_0\mu+t_0)$, where $\mu$ ranges over the
eigenvalues of $R_n$. By \eqref{eq:projection-approx} and Weyl's
inequality, at most $r_n$ of these $\mu$ exceed $n^{-20}/s_0$, so
$\operatorname{tr} B_s\le b_n^{-p/2}(r_n/s_0+n^{-19}/(s_0t_0))\le C\epsilon_n^{-1}$.
Hence $\operatorname{tr}(B_s^3)\ge c\epsilon_n$, and
$\partial_{h_s}^3L_n(0)\ge c\epsilon_n$ with probability tending to one,
after decreasing $c$.

For the fourth derivative, all matrices involved commute with $R_n$. In
an eigenbasis of $R_n$, with $Y_n$ having independent coordinates of
variances $s_0\mu_i+t_0$, each eigenvalue of $C^{-1}R_n$ is at most
$C\min(1,\mu_i)$ for $|\sigma-s_0|\le s_0/2$. Therefore
$\sup_{|\sigma-s_0|\le s_0/2}|\partial_\sigma^4l|$ is bounded by a
constant times $\sum_i\min(1,\mu_i^4)(1+\chi_i^2)$ with $\chi_i$
independent standard normal, which is $O_{\mathbb P}(r_n)$ by the eigenvalue
count above. After normalization, the fourth derivative in $h_s$ is
$O_{\mathbb P}(b_n^{-2p}r_n)=O_{\mathbb P}(\epsilon_n^2)$ uniformly on
$|u|\le\kappa\epsilon_n^{-1/3}$.

Now let $u=\kappa\epsilon_n^{-1/3}$, so that $\sigma-s_0=\kappa\epsilon_n^{2/3}\to0$.
Taylor's formula in $u$, together with \eqref{eq:hessian-local}, gives
\[
 L_n(ue_s)-L_n(0)-u\Delta_{n,s}+\frac12J_{n,ss}u^2
 =O_{\mathbb P}(\epsilon_nu^2)+\frac16\partial_{h_s}^3L_n(0)\,u^3
 +O_{\mathbb P}(\epsilon_n^2u^4).
\]
The first and last terms are $O_{\mathbb P}(\kappa^2\epsilon_n^{1/3})$ and
$O_{\mathbb P}(\kappa^4\epsilon_n^{2/3})$, and the middle term is at least
$c\kappa^3/6$ with probability tending to one. This proves
\Cref{rem:radius}.

body_md:
Use $X_n$ and $B_a$ from the preceding proof. For a fixed
$v\in\mathbb R^3$, write
\[
 v^\top M_n^{-\top}\nabla l_n(\theta_0)
 =\frac12\{X_n^\top B_n(v)X_n-\operatorname{tr} B_n(v)\},
\]
where
\[
 B_n(v)=\sum_a[D_nM_n^{-1}v]_a B_a.
\]
Since $M_n^{-1}M_n^{-\top}=(M_n^\top M_n)^{-1}=\mathcal I_n(\theta_0)^{-1}$ and
$\mathcal I_n(\theta_0)=D_nJ_nD_n$,
\[
 (D_nM_n^{-1})(D_nM_n^{-1})^\top=D_n\mathcal I_n(\theta_0)^{-1}D_n=J_n^{-1},
 \qquad
 \left\lVertD_nM_n^{-1}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^2=\left\lVertJ_n^{-1}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le C
\]
by \Cref{lem:information}, so the coefficient vector is bounded. Hence
$\left\lVertB_n(v)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_v\epsilon_n\to0$.
The variance is exactly
$\frac12\operatorname{tr}(B_n(v)^2)
=v^\top M_n^{-\top}\mathcal I_n(\theta_0)M_n^{-1}v=\left\lVertv\right\rVert^2$.

For $v\ne0$, diagonalize the symmetric matrix $B_n(v)$, with
eigenvalues $\lambda_{j,n}$. The quadratic form is distributed as
$\frac12\sum_j\lambda_{j,n}(\xi_j^2-1)$ for independent standard
normal variables. Its Lyapunov ratio of order four is bounded by a
constant times
\[
 \frac{\sum_j\lambda_{j,n}^4}
      {(\sum_j\lambda_{j,n}^2)^2}
 \le
 \frac{\max_j\lambda_{j,n}^2}{\sum_j\lambda_{j,n}^2}
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
The univariate central limit theorem and the Cram\'er--Wold device
give \eqref{eq:score-clt}. The same calculation applies to any bounded
sequence of coefficient vectors for $\Delta_n$ whose variances
converge to a positive limit.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $Q$ have side length $L$, and let $A\ge1$ be a fixed constant. For
$n\ge3$, put
\[
 k_n=\left\lfloor\left(\frac{n}{A\log n}\right)^{1/p}\right\rfloor,
\]
and suppose $k_n\ge1$. Partition $Q$ into $k_n^p$ closed subcubes
$Q_1,\ldots,Q_{k_n^p}$ of side length $L/k_n$, which overlap only on
their boundaries. Each has volume $L^p/k_n^p$, so its sampling
probability satisfies
\[
 \pi_j=\mathbb P(X_1\in Q_j)=\int_{Q_j}f(x)\,dx\ge\frac{f_-L^p}{k_n^p}.
\]
Since $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent and $1-x\le e^{-x}$,
\[
 \mathbb P(\text{no }X_i\text{ lies in }Q_j)=(1-\pi_j)^n
 \le\Bigl(1-\frac{f_-L^p}{k_n^p}\Bigr)^n
 \le\exp\Bigl(-\frac{nf_-L^p}{k_n^p}\Bigr).
\]
A union bound over the $k_n^p$ subcubes gives
\[
 \mathbb P(\text{some }Q_j\text{ is empty})
 \le k_n^p\exp\Bigl(-\frac{nf_-L^p}{k_n^p}\Bigr).
\]
By the definition of $k_n$, $k_n^p\le n/(A\log n)$. Hence
$k_n^p\le n$, because $A\log n\ge1$, and $n/k_n^p\ge A\log n$, so that
$\exp(-nf_-L^p/k_n^p)\le\exp(-f_-L^pA\log n)=n^{-f_-L^pA}$. Therefore
\[
 \mathbb P(\text{some }Q_j\text{ is empty})
 \le n\exp(-f_-L^pA\log n)=n^{1-f_-L^pA}.
\]
Given $q>0$, choose $A\ge\max\{1,(q+1)/(f_-L^p)\}$, so that this
probability is at most $n^{-q}$. When every subcube contains an
observation, every $x\in Q$ lies in some $Q_j$ together with an
observation, so it is within the diameter $\sqrt p\,L/k_n$ of that
observation. Since $\lfloor y\rfloor\ge y/2$ for $y\ge1$,
\[
 h_n(Q)\le\frac{\sqrt p\,L}{k_n}\le2\sqrt p\,L\Bigl(\frac{A\log n}n\Bigr)^{1/p}
\]
on this event, for all $n\ge3$ with $k_n\ge1$. This proves the
probability bound with $A_q=2\sqrt p\,LA^{1/p}$, after enlarging $C_q$ to
cover the finitely many $n$ with $n<3$ or $k_n=0$. With $q=2$, the first Borel--Cantelli lemma proves
\eqref{eq:random-fill}. Since
$(\log n/n)^{1/p}=o(n^{-\kappa})$ for $\kappa<1/p$,
the coverage conclusion follows.
